rows.response:
## The situation in one line
REVL's pressing stimulus (Monday strict press ~65% of sessions, Friday Perform Upper bench ~63%, Sunday Complete overhead ~62%) disappears for the month Ivy is traveling. That's not a scheduling headache — it's an opening. Normally PT pressing work has to be dosed *on top of* REVL's ceiling and watched for the "redundant pressing" trap (Russian-wave + Friday Perform Upper + Sunday Complete = 3–4 pressing sessions/wk) *(revl-class-integration.md §10f)*. This month, PT is the **only** pressing stimulus, so you can program it directly rather than as a capped add-on.

## Training status check (Applied)
"On and off for a year, never consistently" = novice→early-intermediate, not an experienced lifter. Course guidance: **60–70% 1RM for novice→intermediate strength work, ≥80% reserved for experienced lifters** *(Wk07 Ch11 Table 11-10, p29–31)*. This also means a Russian-protocol wave isn't appropriate here (fails the eligibility gate on training history) — this is standard **Movement → Load/Speed** IFT progression, not a strength-block archetype.

## The 3x/week travel-month template (no barbell)
No barbell isn't a real limitation for building pressing strength at this training age — DB/machine/bodyweight press variations cover the multi-joint requirement fine *(exercise order: multi-joint before single-joint, agonist/antagonist pairing, Wk07 Ch11 p13)*. Since hotel-gym equipment will vary, prescribe by **RIR/rep target, not fixed load** — autoregulation *(RPE/RIR as intensity metric, Wk05 Ch8 p15–20)* travels better than a % prescription.

Each of the 3 sessions:
1. **Main press** (DB bench/floor press, DB or KB standing/seated overhead press, or landmine press if available) — 3–4 sets × 6–10 reps @ RIR 2–3, 2–4 s eccentric tempo *(Table 9-12 hypertrophy/strength bands + tempo, Wk07 Ch11 p16–17)*.
2. **One pull movement** (row or pull-up variant) — agonist/antagonist balance, protects shoulder health under rising press volume.
3. **One lower-body/full-body maintenance movement** (goblet squat, split squat, KB hinge) — REVL was carrying squat/hinge (74%/76% of sessions); don't let it fully detrain while paused.
4. Progress via **double progression** — add reps to the top of the range, then bump load ~5% *(2-for-2 rule, Wk07 Ch11 p7, p20; ~5% increments, Wk03 Ch9 p7)*.

Frequency check: 3 direct pressing sessions/week, 48–72h apart, is exactly inside the course's per-muscle-group budget *(2–3 hard sessions/wk, Wk07 Ch11 Table 11-10, p11)* — and with REVL paused there's no overlap to subtract for.

## REVL during travel
Confirm whether Ivy has **any** REVL access on the road, or is fully off it this month — I assumed fully off given the framing, but that changes the dose if wrong (**IMPORTANT gap**, ask before week 2).

## When Ivy returns
Revert to REVL-integration dosing immediately — don't keep running a full 3x/week direct press block on top of REVL. Cap added PT press work back to accessory-level per the current REVL phase (*§12*), and re-apply the redundant-pressing check (*§10f*): a month of dedicated pressing groundwork is what should carry them forward — PT's role shifts back to "different expression" (tempo, unilateral DB, weak-point) rather than volume.

## Gaps worth closing before/while running this
- **BLOCKING-adjacent**: has an ACSM preparticipation screen / PAR-Q+ been run on Ivy at all? Inconsistent training history alone isn't a red flag, but it hasn't been mentioned *(Wk04 Ch5)*.
- **IMPORTANT**: any shoulder/pressing-relevant injury history?
- **IMPORTANT**: REVL access status during travel (above).
- **OPTIONAL**: actual hotel-gym equipment, so I can tighten the exercise menu.

rows.response:
Good timing — REVL's Deload week (week 7 of the 13-week block) is explicitly the best window in the whole block for exactly this kind of work, and there's a course-backed way to run it.

**Why deload week fits**

REVL's Deload is a *strength* deload only — Monday drops to ~8 reps @ 40–50% — but Sunday "Complete" stays dense, so total metabolic volume doesn't drop. That means: excellent window for assessment/corrective/technique work, poor window for adding more high-rep metabolic volume *(revl-class-integration.md §4, §12)*. It also lines up with a real gap in what REVL trains — its data shows unilateral *loading* is common (53–64% of sessions) but unilateral *stability/control* (slow, unsupported single-leg work) is essentially never trained *(revl-class-integration.md §6a)*. A weak, compensating left leg is precisely that gap.

**Session 1 — assess and quantify the asymmetry**

Don't just eyeball it — the course has specific screens for this:

- **Single-leg step-up assessment** (Ch 10, Table 10-17, p48–50) — anterior + side view, both legs. Watch for the compensation pattern on the left specifically: knee caving inward → look for tight adductors/TFL and underactive glute medius; hip hiking or trunk lean → hip flexor/core control; excessive stance-leg internal rotation → weak external rotators. This tells you *what* is weak, not just *that* it's weak.
- **Unipedal Stance Test** (Ch 10, Table 10-10, p23) — eyes-open/eyes-closed hold time, left vs right, compared to age/sex norms. Gives you a numeric baseline to re-test against later.
- **Y-Balance** (Ch 10, p25) only if she has sport/athletic goals — the course notes asymmetry here specifically correlates with injury risk, but it's not appropriate if she has any balance impairment.

Keep everything else in this session light — no heavy squat/hinge work; that's what the deload rule protects.

**Session 2 — build from what you found**

Use the progression continuum the course gives for exactly this situation: bodyweight→machine→free weight, supported→unsupported, bilateral→unilateral *(Ch 11 p19)*. Bias volume to the left leg without abandoning the right — e.g. left-leg-led step-ups, split squats, or single-leg RDL at a supported/lighter rung than her general level, targeting whatever Table 10-17 flagged as underactive, controlled tempo, RIR 3+. This is deliberately sub-maximal — it's diagnostic-driven corrective work, not a new strength stimulus, so it doesn't fight the deload.

**One thing worth asking her before you run this:** is there any pain associated with the right leg compensating, or is it purely a strength/control asymmetry? If there's pain, this routes to Ch 15 (knee/hip region steps) instead, and possibly a PT referral rather than a corrective program — outside scope to treat if it's a genuine injury.

**After this week:** don't try to "fix" it in one week. Use these two sessions to get the baseline (Table 10-17 findings + Unipedal Stance numbers), then carry the left-leg-biased unilateral work into Peak/Rebuild rather than adding it as extra load right when REVL's Peak weeks (8–10) need her fresh.
